title: Domain and Content Delivery Troubleshooting
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of domain and content delivery troubleshooting and its relationship to DNS, Content Delivery, and Edge Services.
Interpret the example and identify at least one prerequisite or boundary relevant to domain and content delivery troubleshooting.
Propose a safe verification or troubleshooting step and record one security, reliability or cost consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn domain and content delivery troubleshooting in the context of DNS, Content Delivery, and Edge Services. You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: Domain and Content Delivery Troubleshooting matters because it is one part of route 53, cloudfront and edge protection. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: Module 9: DNS, Content Delivery, and Edge Services
content_blocks.alt_text: Five-step overview for module 9, DNS, Content Delivery, and Edge Services, followed by verification, least-privilege security, recovery, and cost-cleanup checks.
content_blocks.caption: Module 9 learning sequence: understand the concept, make a controlled design/configuration, verify behavior, and document security/reliability/cost trade-offs.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Domain and Content Delivery Troubleshooting belongs to DNS, Content Delivery, and Edge Services. DNS, edge caching, TLS, origin access and perimeter controls are distinct layers. Diagnose them separately before changing production traffic.

The PDF lists these subtopics: DNS propagation and delegation; Certificate errors; Cache-related deployment issues; Origin access and routing failures. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For domain and content delivery troubleshooting, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

items.title: DNS propagation and delegation
items.text: Trace the path from source to destination through address ranges, routing, gateways and filtering controls. Verify both forward and return paths; one successful configuration screen is not proof of reachability.

items.title: Certificate errors
items.text: Compare the available option with the workload requirement; record the operational, security, availability and cost trade-offs rather than assuming one option is always best.

items.title: Cache-related deployment issues
items.text: Keep the workflow repeatable and reviewable: version the input, validate before applying, inspect changes, protect state/secrets, and specify how to roll back.

items.title: Origin access and routing failures
items.text: Define the failure scenario and recovery objective, then test detection, recovery, data consistency and rollback. Treat recovery evidence as a deliverable, not an assumption.

content_blocks.title: Inspect CloudFront distributions: Domain and Content Delivery Troubleshooting
content_blocks.code:
# Read-only example related to: Domain and Content Delivery Troubleshooting
aws cloudfront list-distributions --query "DistributionList.Items[].[Id,DomainName,Enabled]" --output table
content_blocks.expected_output: A table of CloudFront distribution identifiers, hostnames and enabled status where results are present.

content_blocks.reset_steps: No AWS resource is created by this lesson example. If you independently run an approved lab, capture the starting state first, follow the lab-specific teardown instructions, check dependent resources and billing/resource inventories, and document anything retained.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview and does not execute AWS APIs, shell commands, SQL or cloud deployments. Treat output as illustrative; live values depend on credentials, permissions, Region, service state and schema.

content_blocks.title: Security and cost checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use least privilege, keep Block Public Access/private defaults unless a justified reviewed requirement says otherwise, and document cost/cleanup before live changes.

task: Create a one-page decision card for “Domain and Content Delivery Troubleshooting”. State the goal, prerequisites, the AWS resource or control involved, the expected result, one read-only/static verification step, one failure case, the relevant permission boundary, and cost/cleanup considerations. Do not create or alter billable resources unless the account owner has approved the lab.
hints: Start from the exact subtopics in the lesson and define the desired state in your own words.
Prefer a read-only check or static artifact before a mutating command; record the identity/Region and required permissions.
Verify the expected result and a failure path using current official documentation; write down cost and cleanup implications.
expected_output: A short reviewable decision card for Domain and Content Delivery Troubleshooting with prerequisites, evidence, a failure case, security implications and cost/cleanup notes.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.

summary: Domain and Content Delivery Troubleshooting is taught as part of DNS, Content Delivery, and Edge Services.
DNS, edge caching, TLS, origin access and perimeter controls are distinct layers. Diagnose them separately before changing production traffic.
Verify assumptions with official service documentation and evidence from the relevant AWS resource, logs or tests.
For live labs, confirm permissions and likely charges before acting, then verify cleanup.
